h1: Heart Rate Zone Calculator by Age — 5 Training Zones (Karvonen Method)
description: Enter your age and resting HR to get your exact 5 heart rate training zones (bpm) using the Karvonen method. Includes Z2 fat-burn, Z4 threshold, and VO2-max zones with a reference table by age.
answerSnippet: Your 5 heart rate training zones are calculated using the Karvonen (Heart Rate Reserve) method: HRR = Max HR − Resting HR, then each zone lower = (HRR × intensity%) + Resting HR. For a typical 35-year-old with a 60 bpm resting HR (Tanaka max HR = 184 bpm, HRR = 124): Zone 1 (Recovery) = 122–134 bpm, Zone 2 (Fat Burn) = 134–147 bpm, Zone 3 (Aerobic) = 147–159 bpm, Zone 4 (Threshold) = 159–172 bpm, Zone 5 (VO2 Max) = 172–184 bpm.
intro: Training at the right intensity is what separates burning fat, building an aerobic base, and maximizing VO2 max. This calculator uses the **Karvonen (Heart Rate Reserve) method** — more accurate than simple percent-of-max formulas — to give you five precise bpm ranges based on your age, resting heart rate, and an optional measured max HR. You also get an interactive zone chart and a worked example.
keyTakeaway: Zone 2 fat-burning sits at 60–70% of your heart rate reserve. For a 35-year-old with a 60 bpm resting HR, that's 134–147 bpm using the Karvonen method — roughly where you can still hold a full conversation.

explanation:
## How the Karvonen Heart Rate Zone Calculator Works

Heart rate training zones divide your cardiovascular output into five bands, each targeting a different physiological adaptation. The **Karvonen method** — also called the Heart Rate Reserve (HRR) method — is more individualized than simple percent-of-max formulas because it anchors the lower bound of every zone to your resting heart rate.

## Zone Reference Table by Age (Resting HR = 60 bpm, Tanaka formula)

| Age | Max HR (Tanaka) | Z1 Recovery | Z2 Fat Burn | Z3 Aerobic | Z4 Threshold | Z5 VO2 Max |
|-----|-----------------|-------------|-------------|------------|-------------|------------|
| 20  | 194 bpm         | 127–141     | 141–155     | 155–168    | 168–182     | 182–194    |
| 25  | 190 bpm         | 125–138     | 138–152     | 152–165    | 165–179     | 179–190    |
| 30  | 187 bpm         | 124–136     | 136–150     | 150–163    | 163–177     | 177–187    |
| 35  | 184 bpm         | 122–134     | 134–147     | 147–159    | 159–172     | 172–184    |
| 40  | 180 bpm         | 120–132     | 132–144     | 144–156    | 156–168     | 168–180    |
| 45  | 177 bpm         | 118–129     | 129–141     | 141–153    | 153–165     | 165–177    |
| 50  | 173 bpm         | 116–127     | 127–139     | 139–150    | 150–162     | 162–173    |
| 55  | 170 bpm         | 115–124     | 124–136     | 136–148    | 148–159     | 159–170    |
| 60  | 166 bpm         | 113–122     | 122–133     | 133–145    | 145–156     | 156–166    |

*All values assume resting HR = 60 bpm. Use the calculator above for your actual resting HR.*

## Step-by-Step Calculation

### Step 1 — Determine Max HR

If you have a **measured max HR** (from a graded exercise test or a hard race effort), the calculator uses that directly — it's the most accurate option.

Otherwise, max HR is estimated from age:

```
220 − Age            (classic formula)
208 − 0.7 × Age      (Tanaka et al., 2001 — recommended for adults)
```

The Tanaka formula has a smaller standard error (~7 bpm vs ~10–12 bpm for 220−Age).

### Step 2 — Heart Rate Reserve (HRR)

```
HRR = Max HR − Resting HR
```

HRR represents the full working range of your cardiovascular system.

### Step 3 — Karvonen Zone Formula

```
Zone lower = (HRR × intensity_low)  + Resting HR
Zone upper = (HRR × intensity_high) + Resting HR
```

The five zones and their intensity brackets:

| Zone | Name | Intensity | Purpose |
|------|------|-----------|---------|
| Z1 | Recovery | 50–60% HRR | Active recovery, warm-up |
| Z2 | Fat Burn | 60–70% HRR | Aerobic base, long slow distance |
| Z3 | Aerobic | 70–80% HRR | Cardiovascular fitness |
| Z4 | Threshold | 80–90% HRR | Lactate threshold, tempo runs |
| Z5 | VO2 Max | 90–100% HRR | Maximum oxygen uptake, intervals |

### Worked Example — Age 35, Resting HR 60 bpm

```
Max HR = 208 − 0.7 × 35 = 183.5 ≈ 184 bpm  (Tanaka)
HRR   = 184 − 60 = 124 bpm

Z1: (124 × 0.50) + 60 = 122 bpm  →  (124 × 0.60) + 60 = 134 bpm
Z2: (124 × 0.60) + 60 = 134 bpm  →  (124 × 0.70) + 60 = 147 bpm
Z3: (124 × 0.70) + 60 = 147 bpm  →  (124 × 0.80) + 60 = 159 bpm
Z4: (124 × 0.80) + 60 = 159 bpm  →  (124 × 0.90) + 60 = 172 bpm
Z5: (124 × 0.90) + 60 = 172 bpm  →  184 bpm (max)
```

### Limitations

- **Estimated max HR has ±7–12 bpm error.** A lab or field max-effort test is more reliable.
- Resting HR should be measured after 5+ minutes of quiet rest, ideally on waking.
- Zones are guidelines, not rigid thresholds. Lactate threshold testing gives a more precise Zone 4 boundary.
- These zones apply to running and cycling. Swim HR zones run ~10–15 bpm lower.
- Individuals on **beta-blockers** or other HR-altering medications should consult a physician.

faq.q: What is the Karvonen formula for heart rate zones?
faq.a: The Karvonen formula is: Zone bpm = (Heart Rate Reserve × intensity%) + Resting HR, where Heart Rate Reserve = Max HR − Resting HR. For example, a 35-year-old with Max HR 184 and Resting HR 60 has HRR = 124. Zone 2 lower = (124 × 0.60) + 60 = 134 bpm; Zone 2 upper = (124 × 0.70) + 60 = 147 bpm.

faq.q: How do I find my target heart rate zone by age?
faq.a: Enter your age and resting heart rate into the calculator above. For a quick reference: at age 40 with resting HR 60, the Tanaka formula gives Max HR 180 bpm and a Zone 2 fat-burn range of 132–144 bpm. At age 50 with resting HR 60, Zone 2 is approximately 127–139 bpm. Younger athletes with lower resting HRs will have higher absolute zone values.

faq.q: What is Zone 2 heart rate training and why is it important?
faq.a: Zone 2 (60–70% of heart rate reserve) is the aerobic base zone where fat oxidation is highest and mitochondrial density improves most. Most elite endurance coaches recommend spending 70–80% of total training volume in Zone 2 to build an efficient aerobic engine without accumulating excessive fatigue. It's the zone where you can hold a full conversation.

faq.q: Which max HR formula is more accurate — 220 minus age or Tanaka?
faq.a: Tanaka (208 − 0.7 × Age) is recommended for adults. A 2001 meta-analysis by Tanaka et al. found it has a standard error of ~7 bpm versus ~10–12 bpm for 220−Age, particularly for people over 40. If you have a measured max HR from a recent hard effort or graded exercise test, always prefer that over any formula.

faq.q: How do I measure my resting heart rate accurately?
faq.a: Measure first thing in the morning before getting out of bed, after at least 5 minutes of lying still. Count beats for a full 60 seconds, or use a reliable wearable. Illness, alcohol, caffeine, and poor sleep can elevate resting HR by 5–15 bpm — take readings on multiple calm mornings and average them. A normal adult resting HR is 60–100 bpm; well-trained athletes are commonly 40–55 bpm.

Zone 4 (80–90% of HRR) sits near your lactate threshold — the intensity at which lactate accumulates faster than it can be cleared. Training here raises your threshold pace, meaning you can sustain faster speeds aerobically. Classic formats include 20–40 min tempo runs and 2×20 min cycling intervals at Zone 4 effort.

faq.q: Are heart rate zones different for swimming vs. running?
faq.a: Yes. Swim heart rates are typically 10–15 bpm lower than running HR at equivalent perceived effort, due to the horizontal body position, cooler water, and facial immersion reflex. Apply a correction of approximately −10 to −13 bpm to the zone boundaries for pool swimming. Cycling zones are closely comparable to running zones.

faq.q: What if I am on beta-blockers or heart medications?
faq.a: Beta-blockers suppress both max HR and resting HR, making standard age-predicted formulas and even measured max HR tests unreliable for zone calculation. Use perceived exertion (RPE scale 1–10) or lactate testing under medical supervision instead of HR zones.

faq.q: How often should I recalculate my training zones?
faq.a: Resting HR can improve by 5–10 bpm after 3–6 months of consistent aerobic training, which shifts all zones upward. Recalculate whenever your resting HR changes noticeably, after a significant fitness break, or at the start of a new training block — typically every 3–6 months.

faq.q: What is a good resting heart rate for my age?
faq.a: The American Heart Association defines normal resting HR for adults as 60–100 bpm. For reference: sedentary adults average 70–80 bpm; recreational exercisers 60–70 bpm; trained endurance athletes 40–55 bpm; elite endurance athletes can be as low as 28–40 bpm. Resting HR tends to decrease with age in athletes but can increase in sedentary individuals.
